questions.stem: An attacker sends a fraudulent SMS text message trying to trick a user into revealing credentials. What is this attack called?
questions.explanation: Smishing is phishing carried out via SMS text message.
questions.trap: Vishing is voice phishing over the phone; the SMS-specific term is smishing.

questions.stem: A malicious QR code on a parking meter sends users to a fake payment site. Which social-engineering attack is this?
questions.explanation: QR code phishing (quishing) uses malicious QR codes to send victims to fake sites.
questions.trap: Vishing is voice-based; the QR-code vector is quishing.

questions.stem: An attacker crafts a highly targeted phishing email aimed at the company's CFO specifically. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Targeting a senior executive (a 'big fish' like the CFO) is whaling. Spear phishing targets specific individuals; whaling is spear phishing aimed at a high-level executive.
questions.trap: General phishing casts a wide net; the executive-specific targeting here is whaling, not generic phishing.

questions.stem: An employee holds a secure door open for someone carrying boxes who lacks their own badge. Which attack does this enable?
questions.explanation: Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secure door without valid access of your own.
questions.trap: Shoulder surfing is watching someone enter credentials; it does not involve physically following through a door.

questions.stem: An attacker secretly positions themselves between a user and a server, intercepting traffic. On a local network this is often done via ARP spoofing. What is the general attack called?
questions.explanation: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack secretly intercepts traffic between two parties; ARP spoofing is a common local-network method.
questions.trap: A denial of service makes a service unavailable; it does not quietly intercept traffic in transit.

questions.stem: At an airport, a rogue access point broadcasts the same network name as the legitimate Wi-Fi to trick devices into connecting. What is this called, and what defends against it?

choices.text: Evil twin; use a VPN on public Wi-Fi
Zero day; apply a vendor patch

questions.explanation: An evil twin is a rogue AP using the legitimate network's name. Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi protects your traffic even if you connect to one.
questions.trap: Brute force targets passwords; it is unrelated to a rogue access point impersonating a network name.

questions.stem: A web login box is exploited by typing malicious database commands into the field, potentially bypassing authentication. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: SQL injection exploits a site's database by entering malicious SQL into an input field, potentially bypassing authentication.
questions.trap: XSS injects malicious JavaScript that runs in the victim's browser; SQL injection targets the database via input fields.

questions.stem: An attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a legitimate website so it runs in visitors' browsers, often to steal session cookies. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects malicious JavaScript into a legitimate site so it executes in the victim's browser, often to steal the session cookie.
questions.trap: SQL injection targets the database via input fields; XSS targets the user's browser via injected scripts.

questions.stem: Attackers compromise a trusted third-party HVAC vendor to ultimately steal a major retailer's VPN credentials. Which attack category is this?
questions.explanation: A supply chain attack compromises a trusted third-party vendor to reach the real target.
questions.trap: A zero-day exploits an unpatched vulnerability directly; here the path runs through a trusted vendor, which is supply chain.

questions.stem: Which vulnerability is described as the MOST dangerous because the vendor no longer provides any security updates for the system?
questions.explanation: End-of-life systems are the most dangerous because the vendor no longer issues security updates, so new flaws are never patched.
questions.trap: An unpatched supported system is risky but can still receive patches; an EOL system cannot, which is worse.
